title: Safe Stack
story: Stack underflow crashes are among the most common runtime errors in systems programming — calling `pop()` on an empty stack is undefined in many languages. Contracts make this impossible.
why: Contracts on data structure operations make misuse a compile-time or immediately-trapped error, never a silent corruption.
analogy: A contract is the 'You must be this tall to ride' sign. The Option is the seatbelt once you're on. Both protect you, at different levels.
try_it: Add a `Stack.is_empty` method that returns `Bool` and does NOT require a contract (it's always safe). Then add `Stack.size` with an `ensures: result >= 0` contract.
tips: Use `requires` for preconditions that must be met by the CALLER before calling the function
Use `ensures` with `@pre` to document how the function changed the state
Return `Option` even when contracts guard the precondition — it keeps the type signature honest
common_mistakes: Calling `pop()` without checking `len() > 0` — the contract catches it, but you shouldn't rely on failures for control flow
Writing `ensures` without `@pre` when you're comparing post-state to pre-state
Forgetting to use `&mut Self` on mutating methods — the contract won't save you from the borrow checker
